title: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
text:
- 1. Biggest IPO in history, but it’s not all good news Closing the day about 17% higher than its initial public offering price, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 when the market closed taking its valuation to roughly $1.7tn. The share price initially soared by 34% when trading got under way on Thursday, briefly taking the company’s valuation to more than $2tn. The blockbuster debut easily places the IPO as the biggest in history, with the 980m shares sold raising $81bn, surpassing the previous record held by Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s $75bn raised in June. Despite the excitement, major US stock indexes fells to seven-month lows on Thursday, dragged down by growing concerns about the longer-term outlook for the AI industry. “The blockbuster Anthropic launch is a critical step in reassuring the market about the potential for AI, but it’s really just the beginning,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. 
 We still need to see what happens with OpenAI, how the Nvidia situation evolves, how the political climate for data centres shapes up, and what the historical performance for Anthropic proves to be before we’ll get any real sense of stability.”
In early trading on Friday, Asian stocks plunged by up to 4%, suggesting Anthropic’s debut has done little to settle nerves on trading floors.
- 2. A staggering rise in revenue ... and debt According to reports demand for Anthropic shares was about six times what the company was able to offer, an incredible result for a company founded in 2021. Started by a number of former OpenAI employees, Anthropic initially lagged behind its rival frontier lab, but analysts say its focus on building software for business and programming clients has helped to position it as one of the market leaders. That breakneck growth has left investors stunned; from fledgling start-up six years ago, Anthropic is now worth more than US stock market stalwarts Walmart, JP Morgan, Visa and ExxonMobil. The speed of its growth is reflected in its revenue: according to its investor prospectus, Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025. But Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm has said its costs will balloon as it invests further in datacentres. The IPO hands Anthropic a pool of new cash to make those investments, but with promises to spend about $900bn on datacentre infrastructure over the next two decades, experts say their debt is likely to rise even further.
- 3. We need to talk about datacentres Newly minted Anthropic investors will also have to contend with rising public sentiment against AI. Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei has been among the loudest voices pointing out the dangers that the products he and his rivals are developing may pose to humanity. He has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressed concerns that they were being built irresponsibly. Across the US, opposition to AI companies has manifested in protests against local datacentre plans, with a number of municipalities and states voting for bans or restrictions on them at the recent midterm elections. US economic growth is inextricably tied to the booming AI sector, and in particular the vast investments in datacentres that power programmes like Claude and ChatGPT. One estimate from Harvard professor Jason Furman suggested “investment in information processing equipment and software” accounted for 92% of the US’s GDP growth in the first half of 2025.  Any slowdown in that expenditure on datacentres could therefore have far-reaching consequences for Anthropic – and the global economy.
- 4. Democrats eye a crackdown Anthropic’s leaders are also likely looking ahead to the changes to government next year, when Democrats take over both chambers of Congress after securing large majorities in the midterm elections. Senior Democrats have already suggested that tech companies could face a regulatory crackdown over the dangers that advanced AI models pose, and over the volatility that AI IPOs could introduce into the economy. Last month Democrat Elizabeth Warren, a senior member of the Senate banking committee, appeared to signal such moves, telling Amodei in a letter that Anthropic’s IPO “could inject extreme volatility and risk into the financial system, which threatens to undermine Americans’ economic security.” 
 The fact that Anthropic is burning through cash and requires an insatiable stream of capital to feed its growth is not a reason to expose everyday Americans to the company’s risks in our public stock markets … Swings in Anthropic’s share price have the potential to roil the broader markets on day one.”
Jensen Huang – the former CEO of Nvidia, the most important company in providing the advanced chips that power AI – is due to appear before Congress next month. He’ll be answering questions about his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, a scandal that has resulted in the loss of one of Silicon Valley’s key figures and sparked bipartisan national security concerns.
- 5. Open AI next? Earlier this year Anthropic’s chief rival, OpenAI, decided to postpone its initial offering until 2027. Experts say that Anthropic’s market reception and the movements in its share price will act as a signal to others in the industry over what the appetite for another large AI IPO will be. Earlier this week, Open AI CEO Sam Altman said his company will go ahead with the IPO next year, even in the face of increased volatility. Speaking to US publication Semafor, Altman appeared to take comfort from the sheer demand for Anthropic shares, leading up to Thursday’s stock market debut. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply,” he said.
